title: Τὸ τόξον τοῦ Ὀδυσσέως
titleEn: Penelope Brings Out the Bow — Odyssey 21.1–100
about: Book 21 opens with Athena putting a plan into Penelope's mind: she is to set out the bow of Odysseus and a row of axes as a contest among the suitors, and the contest will begin the slaughter. Penelope climbs to the farthest chamber of the house, opens its door with a bronze key, and takes down the great bow, which a guest-friend, Iphitus, once gave to the young Odysseus; the poet tells how the two men met, and how Heracles murdered Iphitus. She weeps over the bow, carries it to the hall, and proposes the contest: whoever strings it most easily and shoots through all twelve axes she will marry. Eumaeus and the cowherd weep at the sight of the bow, and Antinous scolds them, saying that no one there is Odysseus, yet his own heart hopes to string it.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
κούρῃ Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
τόξον μνηστήρεσσι θέμεν πολιόν τε σίδηρον
ἐν μεγάροις Ὀδυσῆος, ἀέθλια καὶ φόνου ἀρχήν.
sentences.l:
And to her in her mind put the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
to the daughter of Icarius, to circumspect Penelope,
the bow for the suitors to set, and the grey iron,
in the halls of Odysseus, a contest and the beginning of slaughter.
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, put it into the mind of the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, to set the bow and the grey iron before the suitors in the halls of Odysseus, as a contest and the beginning of slaughter.
sentences.n: These are the first lines of Book 21, and they hand the story's turning point to Athena: she puts a plan into Penelope's mind. ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε is 'put in her mind', with θῆκε an aorist without augment (Attic ἔθηκε) and φρεσί the dative plural of φρήν, the seat of thought. The plan is the infinitive θέμεν, the epic form of θεῖναι, 'to set (before them)': the bow and the πολιός 'grey' iron are what Penelope is to put out. ἀέθλια and ἀρχήν stand in apposition to the whole act: setting out the bow is a contest, and it is also 'the beginning of slaughter', so the poet tells his hearers at once what the contest will lead to. κούρῃ is 'girl, daughter', and Ἰκαρίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου).

sentences.t:
κλίμακα δ’ ὑψηλὴν προσεβήσετο οἷο δόμοιο,
εἵλετο δὲ κληῗδ’ εὐκαμπέα χειρὶ παχείῃ
καλὴν χαλκείην·
sentences.i: She climbed the high stair of her own house and took in her stout hand a well-bent key, a fine one of bronze;
sentences.n: προσεβήσετο is an aorist middle of προσβαίνω 'step up to, mount', in the epic form in -σετο. οἷο is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν in the genitive, 'her own', and is not the relative: οἷο δόμοιο is 'of her own house'. κληΐς here is a key, a bronze one of bent shape (see εὐκαμπέα, the next word); she uses it in line 47. εὐκαμπέα is 'well-bent', from εὖ and κάμπτω. χειρὶ παχείῃ is 'with a thick hand', a dative of means with Ionic -ῃ for Attic -α; παχύς is 'thick, stout'. The unit stops at the raised dot after χαλκείην, in the middle of line 7.

sentences.t: κώπη δ’ ἐλέφαντος ἐπῆεν.
sentences.l: and a handle of ivory was on it.
sentences.i: and an ivory handle was on it.
sentences.n: κώπη is 'handle' here, the grip of the key. ἐλέφαντος is a genitive of material, 'of ivory'. ἐπῆεν is the imperfect of ἔπειμι (ἐπί + εἰμί), 'was upon it', in the uncontracted epic form (Attic ἐπῆν).

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι θάλαμόνδε σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶν
ἔσχατον·
sentences.l:
She set out to go to the chamber, with attendant women,
the farthest;
sentences.i: and she set out with her attendant women for the farthest chamber;
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι 'set out to go' is a formula of departure: ἴμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἶμι 'go' (Attic ἰέναι). θάλαμόνδε carries the suffix -δε of direction, 'to the chamber'. ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν are two datives, 'attendant women', and ἔσχατον agrees with the chamber that θάλαμόνδε names: 'farthest', the innermost room of the house. The unit ends at the raised dot after ἔσχατον, so line 9 is divided between this unit and the next.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δέ οἱ κειμήλια κεῖτο ἄνακτος,
χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος.
sentences.l:
And there for her lay the treasures of her lord,
bronze and gold and much-laboured iron.
sentences.i: There lay the treasures of her lord: bronze and gold and iron worked with much labour.
sentences.n: οἱ is a dative, 'for her', and ἄνακτος is the genitive of ἄναξ 'lord', that is Odysseus. κειμήλια 'treasures' is formed from κεῖμαι 'lie' and means things laid up; it is neuter plural with a singular verb, κεῖτο, which is ordinary Greek. In the second line πολύκμητος is 'wrought with much toil', from πολύ- and κάμνω. Iron has already been named in line 3, as the 'grey iron' that Penelope is to set out; here it is part of the stored treasure.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ τόξον κεῖτο παλίντονον ἠδὲ φαρέτρη
ἰοδόκος, πολλοὶ δ’ ἔνεσαν στονόεντες ὀϊστοί,
δῶρα τά οἱ ξεῖνος Λακεδαίμονι δῶκε τυχήσας
Ἴφιτος Εὐρυτίδης, ἐπιείκελος ἀθανάτοισι.
sentences.l:
And there the bow lay, back-stretched, and the quiver,
arrow-holding, and in it were many full-of-groaning arrows,
gifts which to him a guest-friend in Lacedaemon gave, having met him,
Iphitus son of Eurytus, resembling the immortals.
sentences.i: There lay the recurved bow and the arrow-holding quiver, and in it were many arrows that bring groaning, gifts that a guest-friend gave him when he met him in Lacedaemon, Iphitus son of Eurytus, like the immortals.
sentences.n: The sentence lists what lay in the chamber and then says where the bow came from. παλίντονος is built on πάλιν 'back' and τείνω 'stretch', so 'stretched back' or 'bent back', and the exact shape is not known. φαρέτρη is the quiver, with Ionic η where Attic has α, and ἰοδόκος means 'arrow-receiving', from ἰός 'arrow' and δέχομαι. στονόεντες is from στόνος 'groaning'. ἔνεσαν is the imperfect of ἔνειμι, 'were in it'. In the gift clause ξεῖνος is the guest-friend, the man with whom a bond of hospitality is shared; δῶκε is an aorist without augment; τυχήσας is 'having met (him)'; Λακεδαίμονι is a dative of place. Εὐρυτίδης is a patronymic, 'son of Eurytus', and ἐπιείκελος takes the dative ἀθανάτοισι, 'resembling the immortals'.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐν Μεσσήνῃ ξυμβλήτην ἀλλήλοιϊν
οἴκῳ ἐν Ὀρτιλόχοιο δαΐφρονος.
sentences.l:
And those two in Messene met one another
in the house of Ortilochus, wise-minded.
sentences.i: The two of them met each other in Messene, in the house of wise-hearted Ortilochus.
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual of the pronoun, 'those two', and ξυμβλήτην is a dual aorist of συμβάλλω, 'met', with ξυ- for Attic συν-. ἀλλήλοιϊν is a dative of 'one another' in an extended epic form. Μεσσήνῃ has Ionic η. δαΐφρων is traditionally 'wise-minded', from δαῆναι 'learn', but the formation is disputed, and a sense 'warlike' from δάϊος 'hostile' has also been proposed; the translation keeps the first. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 16.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἦλθε μετὰ χρεῖος, τό ῥά οἱ πᾶς δῆμος ὄφελλε·
sentences.l:
Indeed Odysseus
came for a debt, which to him the whole people owed;
sentences.i: Odysseus had come about a debt that the whole people owed him;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is 'indeed, truly'. χρεῖος is the Ionic spelling of χρέος 'debt', and μετά with the accusative means 'in quest of, after'. ὄφελλε is the imperfect of ὀφέλλω, here a by-form of ὀφείλω 'owe'; it is not the different verb ὀφέλλω 'increase'. The subject is πᾶς δῆμος, the whole community of Ithaca, which owed the debt as a body; οἱ is a dative, 'to him'. The reason for the debt follows in the next sentence.

sentences.t:
μῆλα γὰρ ἐξ Ἰθάκης Μεσσήνιοι ἄνδρες ἄειραν
νηυσὶ πολυκλήϊσι τριηκόσι’ ἠδὲ νομῆας.
sentences.l:
For flocks from Ithaca Messenian men had carried off
in many-thwarted ships, three hundred, and the herdsmen.
sentences.i: For Messenian men had carried off flocks from Ithaca in ships of many thwarts, three hundred head, with their herdsmen.
sentences.n: The explanation is a raid. μῆλα 'flocks' covers sheep and goats; ἄειραν is the unaugmented aorist of ἀείρω 'lift, carry off'. νηυσί is the Ionic dative plural of ναῦς, and πολυκλήϊσι means 'with many thwarts (rowing-benches)'. τριηκόσι’ is τριηκόσια with its final vowel elided, agreeing with μῆλα. νομῆας are the herdsmen who looked after the flocks, taken along with them.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἕνεκ’ ἐξεσίην πολλὴν ὁδὸν ἦλθεν Ὀδυσσεὺς
παιδνὸς ἐών·
sentences.l:
On account of these a long road went Odysseus,
on an embassy, being a boy;
sentences.i: It was on account of these that Odysseus made the long journey on a mission, though he was still a boy;
sentences.n: τῶν ἕνεκ’ is 'on account of these', picking up the flocks and herdsmen. ἐξεσίην is a mission or embassy, an accusative that sits beside πολλὴν ὁδόν, 'a long road': the journey and the errand are both put in the accusative. παιδνός is a rare Homeric word for 'a boy, boyish' and ἐών is the Ionic participle of εἰμί (Attic ὤν). The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of line 21.

sentences.t: πρὸ γὰρ ἧκε πατὴρ ἄλλοι τε γέροντες.
sentences.l: for forth sent him his father and the other elders.
sentences.i: for his father and the other elders had sent him forth.
sentences.n: πρὸ … ἧκε is tmesis, the preverb πρό standing apart from its verb: together they are προῆκε, 'sent forth', from προΐημι. The object 'him' is not stated and is understood from the line before. ἄλλοι τε γέροντες 'and the other elders' shows that the mission was an act of the community, not a private errand.

sentences.t:
Ἴφιτος αὖθ’ ἵππους διζήμενος, αἵ οἱ ὄλοντο
δώδεκα θήλειαι, ὑπὸ δ’ ἡμίονοι ταλαεργοί·
sentences.l:
Iphitus in his turn horses seeking, which for him had perished,
twelve mares, and under them labour-enduring mules;
sentences.i: And Iphitus, for his part, was looking for horses that he had lost, twelve mares, with labour-enduring mules under them;
sentences.n: The main clause has no finite verb (the only finite verb is ὄλοντο, in the relative clause): Ἴφιτος is the subject and διζήμενος 'seeking' the participle, which is the Homeric form of δίζημαι (Attic ζητέω); the English supplies 'was'. αὖθ’ is αὖτε 'in turn, on his side'. αἵ is the relative, 'which', and οἱ is a dative, 'for him'; ὄλοντο is an unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι 'perish'. θήλειαι is 'female', here mares. ὑπό means 'under'; it is usually taken to mean that the mares had mule foals at their side, but the Greek says only 'under'. ταλαεργός 'labour-enduring' is from τλῆναι 'endure' and ἔργον.

sentences.t:
αἳ δή οἱ καὶ ἔπειτα φόνος καὶ μοῖρα γένοντο,
ἐπεὶ δὴ Διὸς υἱὸν ἀφίκετο καρτερόθυμον,
φῶθ’ Ἡρακλῆα, μεγάλων ἐπιίστορα ἔργων,
sentences.l:
which indeed for him afterwards became both slaughter and portion,
when he came to the son of Zeus, strong-hearted,
the man Heracles, one acquainted with great works,
sentences.i: Those mares became, afterwards, his slaughter and his fate, when he came to the strong-hearted son of Zeus, the man Heracles, who was acquainted with great deeds,
sentences.n: αἳ δή is a relative, 'which indeed', picking up the mares; οἱ is 'for him'. φόνος is 'slaughter' and μοῖρα is the 'allotted portion', which here is a man's lot, his fate. ἀφίκετο takes the accusative, 'came to', and φῶθ’ is φῶτα 'man'. καρτερόθυμος is built on κρατερός 'strong' and θυμός 'heart, spirit' (καρτερός and κρατερός are two forms of one word). ἐπιίστορα is the accusative of ἐπίστωρ, 'one who knows', so 'acquainted with' or 'expert in'; whether 'witness' is also meant is not certain. The sentence is cut here at the comma because it would run past four lines; the relative clause that follows describes Heracles. Line 25 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of ἐπεί, naturally short, must be scanned long to open the line, an unresolved metrical lengthening at foot 1.

sentences.t:
ὅς μιν ξεῖνον ἐόντα κατέκτανεν ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
σχέτλιος, οὐδὲ θεῶν ὄπιν ᾐδέσατ’ οὐδὲ τράπεζαν,
τὴν ἥν οἱ παρέθηκεν·
sentences.i: He killed him, his guest-friend, in his own house, a cruel man, who showed no respect for the gods' retribution, nor for the table that he had himself set before him;
sentences.n: ξεῖνον ἐόντα is 'being a guest-friend', the bond between host and guest; ἐόντα is the Ionic participle of εἰμί. ᾧ is the possessive ὅς, 'his own', not the relative. σχέτλιος is 'cruel'. ὄπις is a rare noun whose sense is not certain; 'retribution' is the traditional guess. ᾐδέσατ’ is the aorist of αἰδέομαι 'show reverence to'. τὴν ἥν οἱ παρέθηκεν is a difficult phrase: τήν takes up τράπεζαν, and ἥν is read as the possessive 'his own'; the sense is the table that Heracles had set before his guest. Killing a guest in the host's own house, after setting a table before him, was a grave breach of hospitality, and the three charges, cruelty, disregard of the gods and disregard of the table, all point at that one act.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτα δὲ πέφνε καὶ αὐτόν,
ἵππους δ’ αὐτὸς ἔχε κρατερώνυχας ἐν μεγάροισι.
sentences.l:
and then he slew him too,
but the horses he himself kept, strong-hoofed, in his halls.
sentences.i: and then he killed him as well, and kept the strong-hoofed horses himself in his halls.
sentences.n: πέφνε is an old reduplicated aorist of φένω 'slay', without augment; it is related to ἔπεφνεν in line 36. καὶ αὐτόν is 'him too, him himself'. κρατερώνυχας is 'strong-hoofed', from κρατερός and ὄνυξ; it is an accusative plural agreeing with ἵππους. μεγάροισι is the dative plural of μέγαρον 'hall'.

sentences.t:
τὰς ἐρέων Ὀδυσῆϊ συνήντετο, δῶκε δὲ τόξον,
τὸ πρὶν μέν ῥ’ ἐφόρει μέγας Εὔρυτος, αὐτὰρ ὁ παιδὶ
κάλλιπ’ ἀποθνῄσκων ἐν δώμασιν ὑψηλοῖσι.
sentences.l:
Those asking after, he met Odysseus, and gave him a bow,
which formerly great Eurytus used to carry, but he to his son
left, dying, in his high house.
sentences.i: Asking after them, he met Odysseus and gave him a bow that great Eurytus had carried before; it was this that Eurytus left to his son when he was dying in his high house.
sentences.n: τὰς ἐρέων is 'asking after those (mares)': ἐρέων is the participle of ἐρέω 'ask', and τάς is a pronoun. Ὀδυσῆϊ is the dative of Ὀδυσεύς, the object of συνήντετο 'met with'. Iphitus is the subject up to δῶκε, which has no augment. In the next line ὁ is a pronoun again, 'he', meaning Eurytus, and ἐφόρει is the imperfect of φορέω 'carry'. κάλλιπ’ is κατέλιπε with the preverb shortened and assimilated, 'left behind'; ἀποθνῄσκων is the present participle, 'dying'. δώμασιν ὑψηλοῖσι is a plural that means one house. The bow therefore passes from Eurytus to Iphitus to Odysseus.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ξίφος ὀξὺ καὶ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ἔδωκεν,
ἀρχὴν ξεινοσύνης προσκηδέος·
sentences.l:
And to him Odysseus a sharp sword and a sturdy spear gave,
a beginning of guest-friendship, caring;
sentences.i: and Odysseus gave him a sharp sword and a sturdy spear, as the beginning of a caring guest-friendship;
sentences.n: τῷ is a pronoun, 'to him'. ἀρχήν stands in apposition to the gift, 'as a beginning'. ξεινοσύνη is 'guest-friendship', the relation of ξεῖνοι, and προσκηδέος agrees with it in the genitive. προσκηδής is a rare adjective built on κῆδος 'care'; the translation says 'caring', but its exact sense is not known. ἄλκιμον ἔγχος is a formula for a sturdy spear. The unit ends at the raised dot after προσκηδέος, in the middle of line 35.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ τραπέζῃ
γνώτην ἀλλήλων·
sentences.l:
But not at table
did the two come to know one another;
sentences.i: but they never came to know one another at table;
sentences.n: γνώτην is a dual aorist of γιγνώσκω, 'the two came to know', and ἀλλήλων is the genitive of 'one another'. τραπέζῃ is a dative of place, 'at table'. The word links back to line 28: Heracles disregarded the table, and here the two men never shared one. The reason follows at once in a πρὶν γάρ clause.

sentences.t:
πρὶν γὰρ Διὸς υἱὸς ἔπεφνεν
Ἴφιτον Εὐρυτίδην, ἐπιείκελον ἀθανάτοισιν,
ὅς οἱ τόξον ἔδωκε.
sentences.l:
for before that the son of Zeus slew
Iphitus son of Eurytus, resembling the immortals,
who gave him the bow.
sentences.i: for before that the son of Zeus killed Iphitus son of Eurytus, who was like the immortals, the man who had given him the bow.
sentences.n: πρίν is here an adverb, 'before that, earlier'. ἔπεφνεν is the same verb as πέφνε in line 29. ἐπιείκελον ἀθανάτοισιν is the accusative of the phrase in line 14. ὅς is the relative, 'who', and refers to Iphitus; οἱ is 'to him', that is Odysseus. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 38.

sentences.t:
τὸ δ’ οὔ ποτε δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἐρχόμενος πόλεμόνδε μελαινάων ἐπὶ νηῶν
ᾑρεῖτ’, ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ μνῆμα ξείνοιο φίλοιο
κέσκετ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι, φόρει δέ μιν ἧς ἐπὶ γαίης.
sentences.l:
And that never heavenly Odysseus,
going to war on the black ships,
took with him; but there, a memorial of a dear guest-friend,
it used to lie in the halls, and he carried it in his own country.
sentences.i: But heavenly Odysseus never took it with him when he went to war on the black ships; it used to lie in his halls, a memorial of a dear guest-friend, and he carried it about in his own country.
sentences.n: τὸ is a pronoun, 'it', the bow. ᾑρεῖτ’ is the imperfect middle of αἱρέω, 'take up for oneself', so 'did not take it'. μελαινάων is an old first-declension genitive plural in -άων (Attic -ῶν), and πόλεμόνδε has the suffix -δε of direction. αὐτοῦ is an adverb, 'there, on the spot'. μνῆμα is 'memorial, remembrance'. κέσκετο is an iterative form of κεῖμαι, 'used to lie', and φόρει is the imperfect of φορέω; both describe a habit. ἧς is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν in the genitive, 'his own', and ἧς ἐπὶ γαίης is 'in his own country'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὅτε δὴ θάλαμον τὸν ἀφίκετο δῖα γυναικῶν
οὐδόν τε δρύϊνον προσεβήσετο, τόν ποτε τέκτων
ξέσσεν ἐπισταμένως καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνεν,
ἐν δὲ σταθμοὺς ἄρσε, θύρας δ’ ἐπέθηκε φαεινάς,
sentences.l:
And she, when now she reached that chamber, heavenly-one of women,
and mounted the oaken threshold, which once a carpenter
planed skilfully and straightened to the line,
and in it fitted posts, and set on shining doors,
sentences.i: When she, heavenly among women, had come to that chamber and mounted the oaken threshold, which a carpenter had once planed skilfully and trued straight to the line, and had fitted posts into it and hung shining doors upon it,
sentences.n: This sentence has a long subordinate part and its main verb comes in line 46. ἡ is a pronoun, 'she'; θάλαμον τὸν is 'that chamber' (the pronoun again), while τόν in the next line is the relative 'which'. δῖα γυναικῶν is the formula for Penelope. οὐδὸν δρύϊνον is the 'oaken threshold'. Line 44 has been heard before, of the ashwood threshold at which Odysseus sat; this threshold is oaken, and the same words describe the carpenter’s craft. σταθμούς is the accusative plural of σταθμός 'post' (of a door), a different word from στάθμη 'carpenter's line' in line 44, though both come from the root of ἵστημι 'stand'. ἄρσε is the aorist of ἀραρίσκω 'fit', and φαεινάς is 'shining'. The unit is cut at the comma after line 45 because the sentence runs on to line 48.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ ἥ γ’ ἱμάντα θοῶς ἀπέλυσε κορώνης,
ἐν δὲ κληῗδ’ ἧκε, θυρέων δ’ ἀνέκοπτεν ὀχῆας
ἄντα τιτυσκομένη·
sentences.i: she swiftly slipped the strap from the handle, thrust in the key, and drove back the bolts of the doors, aiming straight at them;
sentences.n: ἥ γ’ is 'she' and ἱμάς is 'strap'; the strap was looped over a κορώνη, literally a 'crow' and a name for anything curved, here the handle of the door, and she loosens it before using the key. ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι, 'sent in'. ἀνέκοπτεν is the imperfect of ἀνακόπτω, 'strike back', and ὀχῆας is the accusative plural of ὀχεύς 'bolt'. ἄντα means 'straight against' and τιτυσκομένη is 'aiming'. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of line 48.

sentences.t:
τὰ δ’ ἀνέβραχεν ἠΰτε ταῦρος
βοσκόμενος λειμῶνι·
sentences.l:
and they bellowed up like a bull
grazing in a meadow;
sentences.i: and they bellowed like a bull grazing in a meadow;
sentences.n: τά is a neuter plural, 'they': the doors or their bolts, the Greek does not choose between them. ἀνέβραχεν is the aorist of ἀναβράχω, a verb for a loud clashing or roaring noise; a neuter plural takes a singular verb. ἠΰτε is 'like, as', and βοσκόμενος 'grazing' is a present middle participle. The comparison is of sound only: the noise of the bolts and doors is likened to a bull’s bellowing.

sentences.t:
τόσ’ ἔβραχε καλὰ θύρετρα
πληγέντα κληΐδι, πετάσθησαν δέ οἱ ὦκα.
sentences.l:
so loud bellowed the fine doors
when struck by the key, and they flew open for her quickly.
sentences.i: So loudly did the fine doors roar when the key struck them, and they flew open for her quickly.
sentences.n: τόσ’ is τόσα 'so much, so loudly', an adverbial accusative. θύρετρα is the plural 'doors', the leaves of the doorway. πληγέντα is the aorist passive participle of πλήσσω, 'struck', agreeing with θύρετρα, and κληΐδι is a dative of means, 'by the key'. πετάσθησαν is an aorist passive of πετάννυμι 'spread out', so 'were spread open'. ὦκα is an adverb from ὠκύς, 'quickly'. Line 49 repeats βράχ- from line 48.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῆς σανίδος βῆ·
sentences.l: And she then upon a high plank went;
sentences.i: and she stepped up onto a high wooden platform;
sentences.n: ἐφ’ is ἐπί with the genitive, 'onto', and ὑψηλῆς σανίδος is 'a high board'. σανίς is a plank, and here a raised floor of boards. βῆ is an aorist without augment, 'went, stepped'. The unit ends at the raised dot after βῆ, in the middle of line 51.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ χηλοὶ
ἕστασαν, ἐν δ’ ἄρα τῇσι θυώδεα εἵματ’ ἔκειτο.
sentences.l:
where chests
stood, and in them incense-scented clothes lay.
sentences.i: where chests stood, and in them lay clothes scented with incense.
sentences.n: χηλοί are chests. ἕστασαν is a pluperfect of ἵστημι with the sense 'stood' (Attic εἱστήκεσαν). τῇσι is the dative plural of the pronoun, 'in them'. θυώδεα is built on θύος, the burnt offering or incense, so 'smelling of incense'. εἵματα is 'clothes' and the neuter plural takes the singular ἔκειτο.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν ὀρεξαμένη ἀπὸ πασσάλου αἴνυτο τόξον
αὐτῷ γωρυτῷ, ὅς οἱ περίκειτο φαεινός.
sentences.l:
From there stretching up, from the peg she took the bow
with the very case, which around it lay, shining.
sentences.i: Reaching up from there, she took the bow down from its peg, case and all, the shining case that lay around it.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν has the suffix -θεν 'from', so 'from there'. ὀρεξαμένη is the aorist middle participle of ὀρέγω, 'having stretched out (her hand)', and αἴνυτο is an imperfect of αἴνυμαι 'take'. πασσάλου is 'peg'. αὐτῷ γωρυτῷ is a dative of accompaniment, 'with the very case, case and all', and γωρυτός is a bow-case. ὅς is the relative, 'which', referring to the case, and οἱ is 'to it' (the bow); περίκειτο is 'lay around'. φαεινός is 'shining'.

sentences.t:
ἑζομένη δὲ κατ’ αὖθι, φίλοις ἐπὶ γούνασι θεῖσα,
κλαῖε μάλα λιγέως, ἐκ δ’ ᾕρεε τόξον ἄνακτος.
sentences.l:
And sitting down there, on her dear knees having set it,
she wept very clearly, and took out the bow of her lord.
sentences.i: She sat down right there, set it on her dear knees, wept in a very clear voice, and drew out her lord's bow.
sentences.n: ἑζομένη is the participle of ἕζομαι 'sit down', and κατ’ αὖθι is a form of κατ’ αὐτόθι 'right there'. θεῖσα is the aorist participle of τίθημι, 'having placed', with the bow in its case as its understood object. φίλοις is the usual 'dear' that Homer applies to what is one's own. λιγέως is the adverb of λιγύς 'clear-voiced', so 'in a clear voice'. κλαῖε is the imperfect of κλαίω, 'wept'. ἐκ … ᾕρεε is tmesis, 'took out', from ἐξαιρέω, and ἄνακτος is 'of her lord'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν τάρφθη πολυδακρύτοιο γόοιο,
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεναι μέγαρόνδε μετὰ μνηστῆρας ἀγαυοὺς
τόξον ἔχουσ’ ἐν χειρὶ παλίντονον ἠδὲ φαρέτρην
ἰοδόκον·
sentences.l:
And she, when she had had her fill of much-wept lament,
set out to go to the hall among the noble suitors,
holding in her hand the back-stretched bow and the quiver,
arrow-holding;
sentences.i: And when she had had her fill of lament and many tears, she set out for the hall among the noble suitors, holding in her hand the recurved bow and the arrow-holding quiver;
sentences.n: Line 57 has been heard before: τάρφθη is the aorist passive of τέρπω, which usually means 'delight' but here 'be satisfied with' and takes the genitive, so 'she had her fill of lament'. πολυδακρύτοιο γόοιο is a genitive in -οιο, 'much-wept lament'. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεναι is the formula 'set out to go'; μέγαρόνδε has the suffix -δε. μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς is the formula 'the noble suitors'. ἔχουσ’ is ἔχουσα 'holding'. φαρέτρην and ἰοδόκον are accusatives and recall line 11. The unit ends at the raised dot after ἰοδόκον, in the middle of line 60.

sentences.t: πολλοὶ δ’ ἔνεσαν στονόεντες ὀϊστοί.
sentences.l: and in it were many full-of-groaning arrows.
sentences.i: and in it were many arrows that bring groaning.
sentences.n: The half-line repeats the end of line 12, ἰοδόκος, πολλοὶ δ’ ἔνεσαν στονόεντες ὀϊστοί: the quiver is described in the same words when Penelope finds it and when she carries it into the hall. ὀϊστός is 'arrow'. The repetition ties this scene to the first.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἅμ’ ἀμφίπολοι φέρον ὄγκιον, ἔνθα σίδηρος
κεῖτο πολὺς καὶ χαλκός, ἀέθλια τοῖο ἄνακτος.
sentences.l:
And with her attendants carried a chest, where iron
lay in plenty, and bronze, contest-prizes of that lord.
sentences.i: Her attendants carried with her a chest in which lay much iron and bronze, that lord's prizes from contests.
sentences.n: τῇ is a pronoun, 'her', and ἅμ’ is ἅμα 'together with', taking the dative; φέρον is an unaugmented imperfect. ὄγκιον is a rare word for a container; 'chest' is a guess from the context, and its exact kind is not known. ἔνθα is 'where'. ἀέθλια is the plural of ἄεθλον 'contest', in line 4 the contest itself; here it more likely means what belongs to contests, prizes, and the translation says 'prizes from contests', though whether they were won or set is not told. τοῖο ἄνακτος is a genitive in -οιο, 'of that lord'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὅτε δὴ μνηστῆρας ἀφίκετο δῖα γυναικῶν,
στῆ ῥα παρὰ σταθμὸν τέγεος πύκα ποιητοῖο,
ἄντα παρειάων σχομένη λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα.
sentences.i: When she reached the suitors, she, heavenly among women, stood by the doorpost of the well-built hall, holding her shining veil before her cheeks;
sentences.n: The three lines are the formula for Penelope's appearance before the suitors, and the English is the same as when they stand elsewhere. στῆ is an aorist without augment (Attic ἔστη), and ῥα is a particle, 'then'. σταθμός is 'doorpost', and τέγεος πύκα ποιητοῖο is 'of the closely made roof', that is the hall. παρειάων is a genitive plural in -άων, 'cheeks', and ἄντα means 'before'. σχομένη is the aorist middle participle of ἔχω, 'holding (up)'. κρήδεμνα is a plural, but one veil is meant; λιπαρά is 'shining, sleek'. Here Murray ends line 65 with a full stop.

sentences.t: ἀμφίπολος δ’ ἄρα οἱ κεδνὴ ἑκάτερθε παρέστη.
sentences.l: and a trusty handmaid then, on each side of her, stood by.
sentences.i: and on either side of her a trusty handmaid took her stand.
sentences.n: ἀμφίπολος is a female attendant, κεδνή is 'trusty', and ἑκάτερθε is 'on each side', with the suffix -θε of place. οἱ is a dative, 'her' or 'beside her'. παρέστη is the aorist of παρίστημι, 'stood by'. Though ἀμφίπολος is singular, ἑκάτερθε points to one attendant on each side.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δὲ μνηστῆρσι μετηύδα καὶ φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.l: And at once among the suitors she spoke, and spoke a speech:
sentences.i: At once she spoke among the suitors, and made her speech:
sentences.n: μετηύδα is 'spoke among', from μετά and αὐδάω, and μνηστῆρσι is the dative plural of μνηστήρ, in the short epic form. φάτο is an aorist of φημί without augment, and μῦθον is 'speech'. Murray prints no quotation marks round speeches; the Greek reader sees the speech begin only from the verbs, and the English opens its quotation marks on the next unit.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες, οἳ τόδε δῶμα
ἐχράετ’ ἐσθιέμεν καὶ πινέμεν ἐμμενὲς αἰεὶ
ἀνδρὸς ἀποιχομένοιο πολὺν χρόνον·
sentences.i: “Hear me, you lordly suitors, who have been pressing upon this house, eating and drinking without pause, always, while the man has been long away;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is a reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear', and μευ is μου, the genitive that it takes. μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες is the formula 'lordly suitors'. ἐχράετ’ is for ἐχράετε, the imperfect of χράω in the sense 'press upon, assail'; the verb is rare, and a sense 'make use of' has also been proposed, so the translation holds to the first only provisionally. ἐσθιέμεν and πινέμεν are infinitives in -έμεν, 'to eat and to drink'. ἐμμενές and αἰεί are both adverbs, 'unceasingly' and 'always'. ἀνδρὸς ἀποιχομένοιο is a genitive absolute, 'the man being gone'. Penelope speaks; the unit ends at the raised dot after χρόνον in line 70.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τιν’ ἄλλην
μύθου ποιήσασθαι ἐπισχεσίην ἐδύνασθε,
ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ ἱέμενοι γῆμαι θέσθαι τε γυναῖκα.
sentences.l:
nor any other
pretext of speech to make were you able,
but eager to marry me and to take me as your wife.
sentences.i: and you could put forward no other pretext in words, but only that you were eager to marry me and make me your wife.
sentences.n: ἄλλην agrees with ἐπισχεσίην 'pretext, excuse'; the word is rare and its sense rests on the context. μύθου is a genitive depending on ἐπισχεσίην, 'pretext of speech', and ποιήσασθαι is 'to make for oneself'. ἐδύνασθε is the imperfect of δύναμαι, 'you were able'. ἱέμενοι is the middle participle of ἵημι, 'eager', as in ἱέμενός περ at 1.6. γῆμαι is the aorist infinitive of γαμέω, said of a man 'to marry', and θέσθαι γυναῖκα is 'to make (me) your wife'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγετε, μνηστῆρες, ἐπεὶ τόδε φαίνετ’ ἄεθλον.
sentences.l: But come, suitors, since this contest has appeared.
sentences.i: Come then, suitors, since this contest has now appeared.
sentences.n: ἄγετε is the plural imperative of ἄγω, used as 'come now'. ἄεθλον is 'contest' and φαίνετ’ is φαίνεται 'shows itself, has appeared'; the contest is the one she announces in the next lines. τόδε is 'this'.

sentences.t: θήσω γὰρ μέγα τόξον Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο·
sentences.l: For I shall set the great bow of divine Odysseus;
sentences.i: For I shall set out the great bow of divine Odysseus;
sentences.n: θήσω is the future of τίθημι, 'I shall set (before you)', the same verb as θέμεν in line 3; Penelope now does what Athena put into her mind. Ὀδυσσῆος is a variant of Ὀδυσῆος, with the doubled σ that the metre sometimes needs. θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο, 'divine'.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κε ῥηΐτατ’ ἐντανύσῃ βιὸν ἐν παλάμῃσι
καὶ διοϊστεύσῃ πελέκεων δυοκαίδεκα πάντων,
τῷ κεν ἅμ’ ἑσποίμην, νοσφισσαμένη τόδε δῶμα
κουρίδιον, μάλα καλόν, ἐνίπλειον βιότοιο,
sentences.l:
And whoever most easily strings the bow in his hands
and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes,
with him I would follow, leaving this house,
wedded, very fine, full of livelihood;
sentences.i: And whoever most easily strings the bow in his hands and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes, with him I would follow, leaving this house of my marriage, very beautiful and full of livelihood;
sentences.n: This sentence has the same words that appear in an earlier speech in the poem. ὃς δέ κε … ἐντανύσῃ is 'whoever strings': κε with the subjunctive makes a general condition. ῥηΐτατ’ is the superlative adverb ῥηΐτατα 'most easily'. διοϊστεύσῃ is 'shoots an arrow through', here with the genitive πελέκεων 'of axes', and the number twelve is given by δυοκαίδεκα. ἑσποίμην is the aorist optative of ἕπομαι, 'I would follow', and νοσφισσαμένη is the aorist middle participle of νοσφίζομαι, 'leaving'. κουρίδιον is 'wedded', of the house of her marriage as a young bride, and ἐνίπλειον is 'full of'. βιότοιο is the genitive of βίοτος, 'livelihood'. The sentence runs to line 79; it is cut at the end of line 78 because it would pass four lines.

sentences.t: τοῦ ποτὲ μεμνήσεσθαι ὀΐομαι ἔν περ ὀνείρῳ.
sentences.l: of it some day I think I shall remember, even in a dream.”
sentences.i: I think I shall remember it one day, even in a dream.”
sentences.n: τοῦ is the genitive 'of it', the house, the object of μεμνήσεσθαι, which takes the genitive. ὀΐομαι is 'I think', and ἔν περ ὀνείρῳ is 'even in a dream', with περ giving the force of 'even'. This closes Penelope's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, καί ῥ’ Εὔμαιον ἀνώγει, δῖον ὑφορβόν,
τόξον μνηστήρεσσι θέμεν πολιόν τε σίδηρον.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and Eumaeus she bade, the heavenly swineherd,
the bow for the suitors to set, and the grey iron.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and she bade Eumaeus, the heavenly swineherd, to set the bow and the grey iron before the suitors.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the formula that ends a speech. ἀνώγει is a form of the old perfect-present ἄνωγα 'I bid', here with past sense, 'she bade'. δῖον ὑφορβόν is the formula 'heavenly swineherd'. Line 81 is line 3 word for word: what Athena put into Penelope's mind is now commanded, and carried out by Eumaeus.

sentences.t: δακρύσας δ’ Εὔμαιος ἐδέξατο καὶ κατέθηκε·
sentences.l: And weeping, Eumaeus received them and set them down;
sentences.i: And Eumaeus, weeping, took them and set them down;
sentences.n: δακρύσας is the aorist participle of δακρύω, 'having burst into tears'. ἐδέξατο is the aorist middle of δέχομαι, 'received', and κατέθηκε is 'set down'. The bow and the iron are not stated as objects but are understood from line 81.

sentences.t: κλαῖε δὲ βουκόλος ἄλλοθ’, ἐπεὶ ἴδε τόξον ἄνακτος.
sentences.l: and the cowherd wept elsewhere, since he saw the bow of his lord.
sentences.i: and the cowherd wept in another place when he saw his lord's bow.
sentences.n: βουκόλος is 'cowherd'; he is not named in these lines. ἄλλοθ’ is ἄλλοθι 'elsewhere', with the suffix -θι of place. ἴδε is an aorist without augment (Attic εἶδε), and ἄνακτος is the genitive of ἄναξ, 'lord'. The tears of the two herdsmen are the cue for Antinous.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l: And Antinous rebuked them, and spoke a word and called them by name:
sentences.i: And Antinous rebuked them, and spoke, calling them by name:
sentences.n: ἐνένιπεν is the aorist of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke', with movable ν, with no object stated; the two herdsmen are meant. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is a formula of address; ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε is tmesis, 'called by name', although the speech that follows uses no names. Antinous is one of the suitors.

sentences.l:
“Foolish countrymen, thinking things of a day,
oh, you two miserable ones, why then do you shed a tear, and for the woman
the heart in her breast stir up?
sentences.i: “You foolish countrymen, whose minds look no further than the day: oh, you two miserable men, why do you shed tears and stir up the heart in the woman's breast?
sentences.n: νήπιοι is 'foolish'; ἀγροιῶται is 'countrymen', men of the countryside. ἐφημέρια φρονέοντες is 'thinking things of a day', with φρονέοντες the uncontracted participle (Attic φρονοῦντες); the sense is that their thoughts go no further than today. ἆ δειλώ is a dual vocative, 'oh, you two miserable ones', and the verbs κατείβετον and ὀρίνετον are dual too, since two men are addressed. νυ is a particle, 'then'. δάκρυ is 'tear' as a collective, and γυναικί is a dative of interest, 'for the woman'. ὀρίνω is 'stir up'. The unit ends at the Greek question mark in the middle of line 87.

sentences.t:
ᾗ τε καὶ ἄλλως
κεῖται ἐν ἄλγεσι θυμός, ἐπεὶ φίλον ὤλεσ’ ἀκοίτην.
sentences.l:
to whom also otherwise
the heart lies in pains, since she lost her dear husband.
sentences.i: Her heart lies in pain as it is, since she has lost her dear husband.
sentences.n: ᾗ is a relative in the dative, 'to whom, whose', and ᾗ τε is the epic relative with τε. ἄλλως is 'otherwise, as it is'. ἄλγεσι is the dative plural of ἄλγος 'pain', and θυμός is 'heart'. ὤλεσ’ is ὤλεσε, the transitive aorist of ὄλλυμι, 'lost'. ἀκοίτης is a word for a husband, 'bedfellow'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἀκέων δαίνυσθε καθήμενοι, ἠὲ θύραζε
κλαίετον ἐξελθόντε, κατ’ αὐτόθι τόξα λιπόντε,
μνηστήρεσσιν ἄεθλον ἀάατον·
sentences.i: Sit and feast in silence, or else go outside and weep, you two, leaving the bow here, a contest that does the suitors no harm;
sentences.n: ἀκέων is 'in silence'. δαίνυσθε is a plural imperative, addressed to all the company, while κλαίετον, ἐξελθόντε and λιπόντε are dual, aimed at the two herdsmen. θύραζε has the suffix -ζε (= -δε), 'to the door, outside', and κατ’ αὐτόθι is 'right there, on the spot'. τόξα is a plural meaning one bow. ἀάατον is of uncertain meaning: it is built on ἄτη 'ruin, harm', and 'harmless', 'unharmed' and 'not to be harmed' have all been proposed, and so has the opposite, 'ruinous'; the translation does not know which is meant and uses 'harmless' for want of better. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of line 91.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω
ῥηϊδίως τόδε τόξον ἐΰξοον ἐντανύεσθαι.
sentences.l:
for I do not think
that easily this well-polished bow will be strung.
sentences.i: for I do not think that this well-polished bow will be strung easily.
sentences.n: ὀΐω is 'I think' and takes the infinitive ἐντανύεσθαι, the passive of ἐντανύω, 'be strung'. ῥηϊδίως is the adverb 'easily', from the same root as ῥηΐτατ’ in line 75. ἐΰξοον is 'well-polished', from ἐΰ and ξέω 'plane, smooth'; the adjective agrees with τόξον.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις μέτα τοῖος ἀνὴρ ἐν τοίσδεσι πᾶσιν
οἷος Ὀδυσσεὺς ἔσκεν·
sentences.l:
For there is not among all these any man of such a kind
as Odysseus was;
sentences.i: for there is no man among all of these such as Odysseus was;
sentences.n: μέτα here has its accent drawn back and means μέτεστι 'there is among'. τοῖος … οἷος is 'such … as'. τοίσδεσι is an epic dative plural of ὅδε, 'these', and ἔσκεν is an iterative imperfect of εἰμί, 'used to be, was'. The unit ends at the raised dot after ἔσκεν, in the middle of line 94.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δέ μιν αὐτὸς ὄπωπα,
καὶ γὰρ μνήμων εἰμί, πάϊς δ’ ἔτι νήπιος ἦα.
sentences.l:
But I myself have seen him,
for indeed I am mindful, and a boy, still a child, I was.”
sentences.i: But I have seen him myself, and I remember, though I was only a boy then, still a child.”
sentences.n: ὄπωπα is the old perfect of ὁράω with present sense, 'I have seen'. μνήμων is 'mindful, remembering'. πάϊς is a Homeric spelling of παῖς, 'boy', and νήπιος here has the sense 'child' (elsewhere in this part, 'foolish'); ἦα is the imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). The words claim an early memory of Odysseus, and they close Antinous's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐώλπει
νευρὴν ἐντανύσειν διοϊστεύσειν τε σιδήρου.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, but in him the heart in his breast was hoping
to string the bowstring and to shoot through the iron.
sentences.i: So he spoke, but in his breast his heart was hoping to string the bowstring and shoot an arrow through the iron.
sentences.n: τῷ is a pronoun, 'in him', giving a dative of the person whose heart it is. ἐώλπει is the pluperfect of ἔολπα 'I hope', with imperfect sense, 'was hoping'. ἐντανύσειν and διοϊστεύσειν are future infinitives, 'that he would string' and 'that he would shoot through'. νευρήν is the bowstring. σιδήρου is a genitive, 'through the iron', and the iron is evidently the row of axes of line 76. Antinous's speech has just said that he does not think the bow will be strung easily; the narrator adds that his own heart hoped to string it.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὀϊστοῦ γε πρῶτος γεύσεσθαι ἔμελλεν
ἐκ χειρῶν Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος, ὃν τότ’ ἀτίμα
ἥμενος ἐν μεγάροις, ἐπὶ δ’ ὤρνυε πάντας ἑταίρους.
sentences.i: But he was in fact about to be the first to taste an arrow from the hands of blameless Odysseus, whom he was dishonouring at that moment as he sat in the halls and urged on all his companions.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is 'indeed, in truth', and ἔμελλεν with a future infinitive is 'was about to', the house rendering. γεύσεσθαι is the future infinitive of γεύομαι 'taste', with the genitive ὀϊστοῦ; to taste an arrow is a figure for being struck by it. ἀμύμων is 'blameless', a stock epithet of Odysseus; the true meaning of the word is not known, and the translation keeps 'blameless' without claiming to know why it is used. ἀτίμα is the imperfect of ἀτιμάω, 'dishonoured', and ἥμενος is 'sitting'. ἐπὶ … ὤρνυε is tmesis, 'urged on', from ἐπορνύω. The narrator looks ahead here, as ἔμελλεν signals.
